Multispecialty guidelines recommend ultrasound as the preferred initial study for most patients with suspected nephrolithiasis, with CT used selectively. C
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are more effective and better tolerated than opiates for pain control. B

B Calcium channel blockers may also increase the rate of spontaneous stone passage, although data are conflicting. B

Stones less than 5 mm have a 90% rate of passing spontaneously, and most can be managed conservatively. B The American Urological Association (AUA, 2014, validated in 2019) recommends offering observation for patients with uncomplicated ureteral stones ≤10 mm in size or those with asymptomatic, nonobstructing kidney stones. Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy, and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) are options for stones not passing after 4 to 6 weeks and when there are unrelenting symptoms or signs of infection or sepsis. B

background.definition: Nephrolithiasis refers to the presence of stones in the kidney or collecting system. These stones develop in the kidney and, if small enough, pass through the genitourinary tract without clinical symptoms. Larger calculi cause severe pain when they obstruct urine passage.

list.listitem: The incidence of new renal stones in men aged 40 to 60 years without a prior history is 3 cases per 1000 men/year, declining with age.
For women in their 20s with no prior history, the incidence is 2.5 cases per 1000 women/year, decreasing to 1 case per 1000 women/year by age 50 years.
In one study using two inpatient databases of more than 6 million children, 0.2% had a diagnosis of upper tract calculus (4092 boys and 10,045 girls, sex unavailable for 108).
The lifetime risk of stone formation is 12% in men and 6% in women.
Nephrolithiasis is more common in older white males and less common in younger black females.
Total yearly cost in the United States for management of kidney stones is estimated to be $2.1 billion to $5.3 billion.
A conservative estimate of cost for pediatric kidney stones in the US, based on 2009 annual charges, is at least $375 million.

In a population-based cohort study of 43,516 patients with urinary calculi in Taiwan, the risk of overall cancers was significantly increased (standardized incidence ratio [SIR] 1.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.68-1.83), including a higher risk for cancers of kidney (SIR 4.24; 95% CI, 3.47-5.13), bladder (SIR 3.30; 95% CI, 2.69-4.00), thyroid (SIR 2.50; 95% CI, 1.78-3.40), hematologic origin (SIR 2.41; 95% CI, 1.92-2.99), breast (SIR 1.84; 95% CI, 1.54-2.20), lung (SIR 1.82; 95% CI, 1.59-2.07), digestive tract (SIR 1.69; 95% CI, 1.57-1.82), and head and neck (SIR 1.54; 95% CI, 1.32-1.79).
Kidney stones are also associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease (RR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.14-1.36), stroke (RR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.06-1.38), and hypertension (OR 1.4).

In a large population study, kidney stone formers were at increased risk for myocardial infarction (31%; 95% CI, 2%-69%) after adjustment for chronic kidney disease and other risk factors. Using three prospective cohort studies, women but not men with a history of kidney stones have a higher risk of coronary heart disease. The highest hazard ratio was found in the Nurses’ Health Study II (multivariable HR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.23-1.78).
Stroke risk also appears to be higher in individuals with kidney stones that persisted when removing studies at high risk of bias (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.11-1.23; I2=28.7%;).
Calcium stones: 60% to 80%; precipitated as calcium and oxalate, calcium and phosphate, or a mixture of oxalate and phosphate.
Uric acid stones: 10%. Conditions favoring formation of uric acid stones include low urine pH (eg, excess bicarbonate loss from chronic diarrhea) or uric acid overexcretion (eg, gout and diabetes).

Struvite stones: 10%; occur most commonly when the urinary tract is colonized with certain bacterial strains, including Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Enterococcus, all of which produce urease, which hydrolyzes urea, producing struvite.
Other stones: 1% to 5%; primarily cystine stones (precipitated by drugs, surgically augmented bladders, or a ketogenic diet) or rarely xanthine, indigo, or indinavir.

Twenty nephrolithiasis-associated genetic loci have been identified. A CYP24A1 locus is predicted to affect vitamin D metabolism and correlates with serum calcium concentration and number of nephrolithiasis episodes. Five loci are predicted to influence calcium-sensing receptor signaling.
Hypoparathyroidism can increase risk of kidney stones.

Authors examining causal associations with 45 risk factors using genome-wide significant thresholds found increased odds ratios of kidney stones per standard deviation of 1.21 (1.13, 1.29) in serum calcium, 1.55 (1.01, 2.36) in serum 25(OH)D, 1.14 (1.00, 1.29) in total triglycerides, 2.38 (1.34, 4.22) in fasting insulin, and 0.28 (0.23, 0.35) per unit increase in log odds ratio of urine pH. Other associations with an increased risk of kidney stones were genetically-predicted serum phosphorus, urinary sodium, tea consumption, lower income, less education and waist-to-hip ratio.

Biomarkers of arsenic and cadmium exposures were associated with an increased risk of kidney stones in adults. Odds of kidney stones increased with increasing urinary cadmium, reaching a maximum at 1.50 μg/L (OR 2.56; 95% CI, 1.17-5.59). Similarly, odds of kidney stones increased with increasing total urinary arsenic and urinary dimethylarsinic acid in women, reaching a maximum at 40 μg/L (OR 1.69; 95% CI, 1.08-2.67).

Occupations that may put patients at higher risk of concentrated urine and associated kidney stones include jobs where water intake and bathroom facilities are limited; those requiring more activity while working, especially outdoors; and jobs working in low gravity (mobilize calcium from bone).
Medications that increase the risk of stones include ephedrine, guaifenesin, triamterene, indinavir, zonisamide, and topiramate.

In keeping with current dietary advice, authors of two reviews confirmed the harmful effects of high meat/animal protein intake and low calcium diets. The lowest risk for incident kidney stones was associated with diets high in fruits and vegetables combined with a balanced intake of low-fat dairy products.

Calcium supplementation for osteoporosis does not increase the risk of kidney stones. In the Nurses’ Health Study, higher dietary calcium was associated with a lower risk of incident kidney stones in women.
Although long-term vitamin D supplementation can increase risk of hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, there does not appear to be an increased risk of kidney stones.

Caffeine intake is associated with a lower risk of kidney stones; in the most recent meta-analysis, the pooled relative risk for kidney stones was 0.68 (95% CI 0.61-0.75, I2 = 57%) for the highest category of caffeine intake compared to the lowest. Caffeine increases urinary excretion of calcium, sodium and magnesium, in addition to a diuretic action, with consumption >approximately four cups daily. Tea appears to exert protective effects against stone formation through the accompanying water intake, the action of caffeine, and effects of components with antioxidant properties. In a Mendelian randomization analysis of UK Biobank data, tea intake was causally associated with a decreased risk of kidney stones (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.34-0.66).

However, caffeine appears to increase risk of recurrent stone, with a multivariate-adjusted OR of recurrent kidney stones for per-quartile increment in caffeine intake of 1.15 (95% CI, 1.01-1.31) based on data from the 2007 to 2014 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Risks were higher for women, individuals of non-white race and non-overweight subjects.
Fasting does not appear to be associated with kidney stone formation, although data are limited.
Nephrolithiasis occurs when urine becomes supersaturated with insoluble materials, causing crystal formation.
Stone precipitation occurs with overexcretion or lack of inhibition of the formation of the insoluble combination of calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones.
A urinary pH of less than 5.5 allows uric acid crystallization to occur more easily, while a urinary pH greater than 6.5 favors an increase in phosphate ions.
Heterogeneous nucleation occurs when urate, uric acid, and hydroxyapatite crystals form with calcium and phosphate adhering to the nucleus.

Randall plaques are subepithelial calcification of the renal papilla. In a study from France, investigators observed a dramatic increase in Randall plaque-associated renal stones, particularly in young patients, associated with increased osteocalcin serum levels, suggesting an altered vitamin D response.

Authors of a systematic review of 25 studies found that the gut microbiota profile of adults with kidney disease and kidney stones differs from controls. Adults with kidney stones had variations to Bacteroides, Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 group, Ruminiclostridium 5 group, Dorea, Enterobacter, and Christensenellaceae.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies including 356 patients with nephrolithiasis and 347 healthy subjects found a higher abundance of Bacteroides (35.11% vs 21.25%) and Escherichia Shigella (4.39% vs 1.78%), and a lower abundance of Prevotella_9 (8.41% vs 10.65%) in the gut microbiota among stone formers. Qualitative analyses identified 10 taxa (Bacteroides, Phascolarctobacterium, Faecalibacterium, Flavobacterium, Akkermansia, Lactobacillus, Escherichia coli, Rhodobacter and Gordonia) that helped in the detection of kidney stones.
For preventing recurrence of stones, increasing hydration to achieve a urine output of 2 L or greater per day may decrease kidney stone formation ( RR 0.45). B

Secondary prevention for patients with a first renal stone include increased water intake; B under certain circumstances, restriction of salt, protein, and oxalate; B and use of thiazide diuretics, potassium citrate, allopurinol, or acetohydroxamic acid. A

Authors of a 2020 Cochrane review found that increased water intake may reduce the risk of stone recurrence and prolong the average time interval for recurrences. Despite weak evidence, the American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends increased fluid intake throughout the day to achieve at least 2 L of urine per day to prevent recurrent kidney stones, and the AUA recommends fluid intake to achieve a urine volume of at least 2.5 liters daily for all stone formers.

A diet with reduced salt (<50 mmol/d) and low protein (<52 g/d) decreases recurrence in patients with hypercalciuria. The AUA recommends that patients with calcium stones and relatively high urinary calcium limit sodium intake and consume 1,000 to 1,200 mg/day of dietary calcium.

Consuming animal protein, including fish, is associated with increased serum and urine uric acid. Patients with uric acid stones or calcium stones and relatively high urinary uric acid should consider limiting intake of non-dairy animal protein.

There is some evidence that reducing dietary oxalate in patients with calcium oxalate stones (eg, spinach, rhubarb, chocolate, nuts) and maintaining normal calcium consumption can reduce stone formation. Low calcium intake may precipitate calcium oxalate stones.
Increase fruits and vegetables can be used to raise urine citrate levels which may reduce risk for some renal stones .
Consuming coffee, beer, wine, and tea have been associated with a decreased risk of renal stones.

listitem.strong: Drug therapy or supplements to prevent recurrence

list.listitem: If urate stones recur in a patient with hyperuricemia, consider allopurinol to lower uric acid levels, although good evidence from RCTs is lacking. The AUA, 2014 recommends against routinely offering allopurinol as first-line therapy to patients with uric acid stones.

Thiazide diuretics (eg, 50 mg/day or more of hydrochlorothiazide) are an option to reduce the recurrence of calcium stones in patients with hypercalciuria
Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 571 patients found a pooled RR for incidence of recurrent kidney stones of 0.44, 95% CI, 0.33-0.58 in the thiazide diuretic groups compared to placebo and untreated groups. However, study quality was low and those randomized to thiazide treatment had a high incidence of adverse reactions and low drug tolerance.

Among patients with several stone recurrences, once daily hydrochlorothiazide appears ineffective. In an RCT including 416 primarily white male adults with at least 2 episodes of calcium-containing kidney stones in the past 10 years, 59% of participants experienced a symptomatic or radiologic stone at a median follow-up of 2.9 years, but there was no difference between groups receiving any of three doses of hydrochlorothiazide compared to placebo.

Potassium–magnesium citrate given daily reduces the recurrence of calcium oxalate stones. The AUA recommends potassium citrate therapy for patients with recurrent calcium stones and low or relatively low urinary citrate.
For patients with recurrent struvite stones, the AUA suggests offering acetohydroxamic acid (AHA) after surgical options have been exhausted.

The ACP recommends pharmacologic monotherapy with a thiazide diuretic, citrate, or allopurinol to prevent recurrent kidney stones in patients with active disease for whom increased fluid intake fails to reduce stone formation.
In children with renal stones, oral potassium citrate supplementation may reduce the risk of recurrence based on a Cochrane review, although the quality of studies was limited.
Acute colicky pain with nausea and vomiting, combined with costovertebral angle tenderness and microscopic hematuria, is highly predictive of nephrolithiasis. C

The most accurate test for diagnosis is helical CT without contrast. Ultrasound is less accurate for smaller and distal ureter stones, but has no radiation exposure and is therefore recommended as the initial study for most patients. C

Patients with known disease; pain with sickle cell disease usually more localized in the abdomen
Pain is less acute; pain in appendicitis usually begins periumbilically with anorexia as a complaint
History, associated triggers and symptoms, radiologic findings
Older patients with risk factors; pain radiating to the back; radiologic findings

list.listitem: Classic history includes sudden onset of unilateral flank pain that waxes and wanes in intensity. As the stone progresses distally in the ureter, the pain tends to migrate caudally and medially.
The most significant predictors of acute renal colic include dysuria, flank pain, decreased appetite, and sudden onset.
Other presenting symptoms include urinary frequency and urgency, particularly with stones located at the junction of the bladder and the ureter.
Rarely, patients may report gross hematuria without pain. Absence of hematuria does not rule out renal stones (occurs in about 10% of patients with stones).
Physical examination often reveals a patient in "colicky" pain unable to find a comfortable position. Costovertebral angle pain may be present.
If the obstructed stone has caused infection, then fever, chills, and other symptoms of sepsis may be present.
In women of childbearing age, a pregnancy test should be done before choosing imaging studies.

Blood test results are typically normal, although an increase in white blood cells may be present with infection. Serum chemistries are useful to evaluate for kidney function (creatinine, BUN) and metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate and chloride levels). Measure levels of uric acid to assess for hyperuricemia and screen for hyperparathyroidism with a serum calcium level.
A high serum calcium of >10.2 mg/dL has a high positive and low negative likelihood ratio for primary hyperparathyroidism, especially if combined with a serum PTH >65 ng/dL.

The AUA 2014/2019 guideline on medical management of kidney stones recommends obtaining a serum intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) level as part of the screening evaluation if primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Based on expert opinion, metabolic testing should be performed in high-risk or interested first-time stone formers and recurrent stone formers consisting of one or two 24-hour urine collections obtained on a random diet and analyzed at minimum for total volume, pH, calcium, oxalate, uric acid, citrate, sodium, potassium and creatinine.

Prior to surgical procedures, the AUA suggests obtaining a complete blood count and platelet count for patients for whom there is a significant risk of hemorrhage or symptoms suggesting anemia, thrombocytopenia, or infection, and serum electrolytes and creatinine if there is suspicion of reduced renal function.

Urinalysis often reveals red blood cells, although in a study of 267 patients presenting with acute flank pain, 11% of patients with renal lithiasis had no red blood cells in the urine. Urinalysis may reveal specific crystals indicative of the type of stone present.
The AUA recommends obtaining a urinalysis prior to any procedure for kidney stones.

For patients with recurrent stones of unknown origin, a single 24-hour urine collection at 4 to 6 weeks after stone resolution while the patient is on a home diet without restriction is the most cost-effective approach. The urine should be screened for total urine volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, phosphorous, creatinine, and cystine.
Stone material passed or retrieved should be sent for analysis.
Imaging options include plain radiographs of the kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB); ultrasound (recommended for most patients); noncontrast helical CT; and IV pyelogram (IVP).

Plain films are a reasonable option for patients with a history of previous radiopaque stones that have been visible on KUB. Plain films can miss stones in the middle section of ureter and can also miss radiolucent calculi (mainly uric acid stones).

Ultrasound (US) spares the patient radiation exposure (particularly important during pregnancy) but only visualizes the kidney and proximal ureter and may miss distal ureteral stones; ultrasound may also miss stones less than 3 mm in size and may overestimate size of stones in the 0 to 10 mm range. The sensitivity and specificity of renal US is 54% and 91%, respectively. The sensitivity of US to detect ureteric stones and to identify hydroureter is low at 46% and 50%, respectively, but the addition of x-ray KUB abdomen increases the sensitivity for ureteric stones to 77%. There was a significant association between sensitivity of US and stone size, but not with stone location. US significantly overestimated stone size. US is excellent for identifying associated hydronephrosis, with 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity.
Ultrasound has high specificity in children for the diagnosis of stone (LR+ 76).

An expert panel composed of representatives from the American College of Emergency Physicians, American College of Radiology, and AUA concluded that US was preferred intial imaging in most situations, including patients with a first stone (8/9 members agreed). CT was preferred for patients age 75 years and older, cases for which ultrasound imaging is nondefinitive, or patients with a stone that does not pass spontaneously and an initial CT scan was not performed.

Noncontrast helical CT is the reference standard but does not provide information on kidney function. IVP, while less sensitive and specific, does provide information on kidney anatomy and function. There is greater than 95% sensitivity and specificity of low dose CT for renal stones.

Noncontrast helical CT is considered the best option in a patient with acute flank pain and suspicion of stone according to the 2023 American College of Radiology (ACR) guidelines. Other options, rated as possibly appropriate are ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder retroperitoneal or radiography abdomen/pelvis. ACR recommends ultrasound as the initial test for pregnant women and in the emergent setting for acute management to evaluate for hydronephrosis, but state that for planning an intervention, ultrasound is generally not adequate and CT is complementary.

The AUA guideline (2016) on surgical management of stones recommends obtaining noncontrast CT prior to performing percutaneous nephrolithotomy and suggests obtaining this test to help select the best candidate for extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) versus ureteroscopy.

It may be possible to differentiate uric acid from non-uric acid renal stones using two consecutive and spatially-registered conventional CT scans. Authors of a study examining various dual-energy CT (DECT) technologies for determining renal stone composition found that all scanners except twin-beam DECT had an AUC >0.95 in at least one acquisition in distinguishing urate from other stones. All DECT techniques were able to help differentiate calcium oxalate monohydrate stones with moderate accuracy (AUC: 0.70-0.83) and brushite differentiated from urate with AUC >0.99.

Some findings on non-contrast CT may be useful for predicting successful ESWL. Based on a meta-analysis, these are Hounsfield unit and density (softer stones more amenable), skin to stone distance, ureteral wall thickness, stone volume and area, abdominal fat parameters, diameter of proximal ureter, and hydronephrosis.

listitem.strong: Comparing US-first to CT-first approaches to diagnosis

list.listitem: In one large RCT, a strategy of initial radiology-department or point-of-care ultrasound was a safe and accurate diagnostic approach for patients with clinically suspected kidney stones compared with initial CT. More patients receiving point-of-care ultrasound underwent subsequent imaging than those randomized to radiology-department ultrasound (41% vs. 27%, respectively). CT was more sensitive but increased radiation exposure.

In an RCT of implementation of an ultrasound-first clinical decision support (CDS) tool in patients with suspected nephrolithiasis presenting to the emergency department, there were significantly fewer CT scans obtained in the 128 patients in the CDS arm compared to the 126 patients in the usual care arm (86.7% vs. 94.4%) and no differences in revisits or hospitalizations at 7 or 30 days.

A cross-sectional, analytical study showed that ureteral wall thickness (UWT) is a non-invasive predictor of stone impaction. Ureteral stones can cause inflammation and edema of the ureteral walls, which increases the chances of impaction. The study used 1.95 mm as the threshold, with patients having UWT less than this threshold more likely to pass stones. However, further studies are needed to define an optimal UWT cut off.

The "four item rule" consists of acute onset of pain (1 point), flank pain (1 point), hematuria (2 points), and positive KUB radiograph (2 points). Among patients with 4 or more points, 90% had stones.
A second clinical rule used five signs and symptoms plus microscopic hematuria to predict the likelihood of stones. This score was 84% sensitive and 99% specific.
See for a suggested approach to the acute evaluation and management of renal and ureteral stones.
Use conservative management for ureteral stones less than 5 mm without signs of sepsis including pain control and increased fluid intake. B

For patients with ureteral stones, alpha-blockers likely increase stone clearance but probably also slightly increase the risk of major adverse events. Alpha-blockers may be less effective for smaller (<5 mm) stones . B
Helpful dietary restrictions include limiting oxalate-containing foods, salt, and protein. B
Consider thiazide diuretics in patients with a first calcium stone and hypercalcuria. B
Use appropriate antibiotics for a UTI when a struvite stone is found. B
Refer patients for ESWL or ureteroscopy for ureteral stones not passing after 2 to 4 weeks; the latter is considered first-line for mid or distal ureteral stones. B

Refer patients for ESWL or ureteroscopy for symptomatic renal stones that fail conservative treatment or for renal stones larger than 10 mm. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is considered for stones that fail removal with ureteroscopy or ESWL or for patients with total non-lower pole renal stone burden >20 mm. C
NSAIDs are effective and better tolerated than narcotics for renal colic pain.

Authors of a systematic review of 12 studies including 2845 adults with acute renal colic concluded that although pain control was similar at 15 minutes for intravenous ketorolac, acetaminophen, morphine or a combination of these drugs, at 60 minutes only those treated with ketorolac had significant pain reduction.

In an RCT including 120 patients with renal colic seen in an emergency department in Iran, adding 8 mg dexamethasone to 30 mg ketorolac was more effective than ketorolac monotherapy in decreasing pain. Fewer patients in the combined treatment arm required a narcotic (35% vs. 58%; NNT 5, 95% CI 3-19) or an antiemetic (12% vs. 28%; NNT 6, 95% CI 4 - 44) during the hour after initial treatment.

Alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists (eg, alfuzosin, tamsulosin, doxazosin, and terazosin) may increase the rate of stone passage by reducing ureteral spasm. In a meta-analysis of 55 RCTs, alpha blockers increased the likelihood of stone passage (number needed to treat [NNT] = 3.74), decreased surgical intervention, and decreased pain episodes. In this analysis, stone passage occurred an average 9.5 days after presentation using alpha blockers compared to 13.3 days without treatment. In a meta-analysis of 8 studies at low risk of bias, tamsulosin increased stone passage over placebo (85% vs. 66%), but there was significant heterogeneity in results, likely due to different stone sizes. Tamsulosin was more effective than placebo for 5-mm to 10-mm distal stones (79% vs. 57%; number needed to treat = 5) .

However, in a large multicenter RCT of 1136 patients with expectantly managed ureteral colic, neither tamsulosin 400 μg nor nifedipine 30 mg were effective for decreasing need for further treatment to achieve stone clearance in 4 weeks.

Calcium channel blockers may increase the rate of spontaneous stone passage, and the combination of an alpha-1 antagonist and calcium channel blocker could have an additive benefit. Based on a review of 5 trials of uncomplicated ureteric stones, tamsulosin was more effective than nifedipine for successful stone expulsion.

Mirabegron (Myrbetriq), a sympathomimetic used to treat overactive bladder, was beneficial for passage of distal renal stones <5 mm in an RCT with 90 patients; stone free rates were higher at all assessment times for the intervention vs. control group (63.6% vs. 33.3% in week 1, 86.4% vs. 54.2% in week 2, and 90.9% vs. 66.7% in week 4).

For patients with cystine stones who are unresponsive to therapy or have large stone burden, the AUA recommends offering cystine-binding thiol drugs, such as alpha-mercaptopropionylglycine (tiopronin).
For prevention of stone recurrence, see "Secondary prevention" above.
For patients with residual or recurrent struvite stones, the AUA suggests offering acetohydroxamic acid after surgical options have been exhausted.
Antimicrobial prophylaxis

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended by AUA prior to stone intervention. The antibiotic choice is based primarily on prior urine culture results and local antibiogram, in consultation with the current Best Practice Policy Statement on Antibiotic Prophylaxis. Guideline.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and two prospective studies including 475 patients undergoing PCNL concluded that one week of prophylactic oral antibiotics based on local bacterial sensitivity pattern plus one dose of IV antibiotics at the time of surgery compared to short-dose preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis reduces the risk of systemic inflammatory response syndrome or sepsis (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.53).

In an RCT of 256 patients undergoing flexible ureteroscopy for ureteral or renal stones, use of a protocol of culture-based antibiotic treatment for positive asymptomatic cases 10 days prior to the procedure and procedure deferral for active UTI was superior to standard antibiotic prophylaxis group (IV fluoroquinolone one hour preoperatively and oral antibiotics for 24 hours postoperatively) for post-procedural UTI; UTI occurred in 8 patients (6.3%) vs. 20 patients in the standard group (15.6%). In addition, the intervention group experienced significantly fewer postoperative and overall complications than the standard-care group (6.3% vs. 15.6% and 17.2% vs. 26.6%, respectively).
The AU has created non-pregnant adult, pregnant adult and pediatric patient profiles to guide surgical management of patients with kidney stones.

A prospective multicenter study evaluating pain before and after removal of non-obstructive renal calculi showed that patients benefited from surgical removal of non-obstructing renal calyceal stones, with decrease in pain and improvement in quality of life at 12 weeks post-surgical intervention.

ESWL is the least invasive procedure and an effective surgical option for calcium oxalate, apatite, uric acid, or struvite stones smaller than 2 cm located in the renal pelvis and for similar stones smaller than 1 cm in the ureter.
AUA notes that ESWL should not be used in a patient with anatomic or functional obstruction of the collecting system or ureter distal to the stone.

In one RCT of patients with lower pole renal stones, adjunctive treatment with external physical vibration lithecbole (EPVL) increased immediate stone-free status following ESWL compared to ESWL alone (76.5% vs. 48.6%, respectively), although stone expulsion rates by week 3 were similar (94.2% vs. 89.2%, respectively).

Ultrasonic stone propulsion for repositioning and facilitating passage of stone fragments is under study. Use of displacement of lower pole stones during retrograde intrarenal surgery prior to lithotripsy resulted in significantly higher stone-free status compared to in situ lithotripsy (95% vs 74%) in an RCT including 138 patients.

Data are conflicting regarding benefit of alpha-blockers on successful elimination of renal stones following ESWL. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for 8 weeks following a single ESWL session was not helpful for improving stone passage in an RCT of 57 patients with a single radiopaque kidney stone of 5-20 mm in diameter. However, in a larger RCT with 235 patients with renal stones ≤ 20 mm or lower calyceal stone ≤ 15 mm amenable to ESWL, the presence of small residual fragments ≤3 mm at 3 months was higher in those randomized to tamsulosin compared to the placebo group (73.8% vs. 59.6%, respectively) as was the absence of any residual stone (43% vs. 15%, respectively), with shorter time to resolution by a median of 6 days. There were no differences in add-on analgesic despite lower numeric pain scores

Ureteroscopic removal of stones (URS) is an option for ureteral stones larger than 5 mm, particularly if distal. A systematic review found that ESWL and ureteroscopy were similarly effective for proximal ureteral stones 5 to 10 mm but that ureteroscopy was preferred for larger stones. AUA recommends ureteroscopy as first-line therapy for mid or distal ureteral stones.
Authors of a meta-analysis concluded that semi-rigid ureteroscopic removal was more effective than ESWL for distal stones, and patients required less retreatment.
Preoperative stenting appears to improve stone-free rates, OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.51-2.58, in patients undergoing flexible ureterorenoscopy based on a meta-analysis of 20 studies with 5852 patients.

Authors of a systematic review of 7 RCTs with 1205 patients who had ureteral stones found a lower stone-free rate (RR 0.84) and lower re-treatment rates with ureteroscopy but less need for auxiliary treatment (5 studies, RR 0.43), fewer complications (RR 0.54), and a shorter hospital stay (2 studies) with ESWL.
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)

PCNL, performed under general or spinal anesthesia, is a technique for stone removal in which dye is placed in the bladder to locate the stone; a small back incision is made; a needle and then guidewire are placed followed by a sheath to allow insertion of the scope; ultrasonic, mechanical or laser lithotripsy is performed to fragment the stone, if needed; the stone is extracted through the sheath; and often a percutaneous nephrostomy tube is placed for drainage.

AUA, 2016 recommends PCNL, laparoscopic, open, or robotic assisted stone removal for patients with ureteral stones that fail removal with ureteroscopy or ESWL. For patients with kidney stones and a total non-lower pole renal stone burden <20 mm, AUA recommends ureteroscopy or ESWL and, for those with >20 mm stone burden, PCNL ().

Infection is the most common complication following PCNL. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found the following were independent risk factors for infectious complications: being female; having a positive urine, renal-pelvis urine, or stone culture; elevated peripheral blood leukocytes or neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; preoperative stent implantation, multiple puncture channels, prolonged operation time, and postoperative residual stones.

Use of contrast-enhanced ultrasonography compared to traditional ultrasound-guided PCNL improved stone clearance rate (OR 2.32, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.68) and reduced puncture time and hospital stays (SMD: -0.37, 95% CI: -0.60 to -0.13), with similar complication rates based on a meta-analysis of RCTs.
Color Doppler ultrasound guidance with a needle bracket reduced hemorrhagic complications in patients undergoing PCNL.

Use of CT urography to assist real-time ultrasound-guided PCNL reduced operative time, lowered rates of blood transfusion, and reduced rates of secondary operation compared to ultrasound-guided PCNL alone in an RCT of 100 patients with renal calculi.

There was no significant difference between day care surgery PCNL and inpatient PCNL for stone-free rates, readmission or overall complications (13.6% and 24.4%, respectively) based on a meta-analysis of one RCT, 4 retrospective case-controlled trials and one prospective cohort study. Patient selection for day care PCNL in the uncontrolled studies likely biases these results.

Tubeless PCNL appears equivalent to standard PCNL with respect to drop in hemoglobin, stone free, blood transfusion and pyrexia based on a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs involving 947 subjects. Patients randomized to tubeless PCNL, however, had significantly reduced postoperative pain, analgesia, hospital stay and urine leakage.

Similar efficacy and reduced hospital length of stay in addition to a lower rate of postoperative urinary fistula was shown in a more recent meta-analysis of RCTs comparing the two procedures. Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found little to no effect on day-one postoperative pain between tubeless and standard PCNL and were uncertain about any differences in other adverse effects although they were able to confirm reduced hospital stay ranging from 1.45 to 0.35 shorter. Comparing totally tubeless (no nephrostomy tube or ureteral stenting) to standard PCNL, there was a reduction in early postoperative pain and severe adverse events based on low-certainty evidence.

Authors of an updated Cochrane review of 31 trials, including 3060 participants with kidney stones who completed follow‐up, found that PCNL was more effective than ESWL for three‐month treatment success with a similar effect on quality of life. ESWL probably leads to fewer complications. ESWL may also have lower three-month success rates than retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS), but there is greater uncertainty regarding quality-of-life outcomes and complications.

Combined PCNL with RIRS (called endoscopic combined intrarenal surgery, ECIRS) appears to offer advantages over PCNL alone for patients with large or complex stones. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 nonrandomized and one RCT found one-step stone-free rates with ECIRS were significantly higher compared with either standard PCNL (OR 5.14, 95% CI 2.54 to 10.4) or mini-PCNL (OR 4.27, 95% CI 2.57-7.1). In addition, use of auxiliary procedures and complication rates were lower with ECIRS.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs with 1832 participants undergoing 6 different interventions, found PCNL superior to other procedures for stone-free rate (OR 3.45; 95% CI, 1.30-9.12), followed by mini-PCNL (OR 2.90; 95% CI, 1.13-7.46). There was a trend for a higher complication rate for PCNL, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 2 RCTs and 9 non-randomized studies with 1618 patients found no differences in stone-free rate, mean operative time, or complications between PCNL and RIRS in which the scope is moved from the urethra retrograde into the ureter. RIRS reduced hospital stay by 1-3 days.

For patients with a single kidney, authors of a meta-analysis of 27 studies (10 PCNL, 1 mini-PCNL, 9 URS, 1 ESWL, and 6 comparative studies) found choice of treatment to be based on stone size, with PCNL, URS, and ESWL offered for mean stone sizes between 25 to 50, 10 to 28, and 12 to 15 mm, respectively. Stone-free rates were similar at 67% to 97.7%, 43% to 100%, and 73% to 80%, respectively, with complication rates of 26.4%, 15%, and 16.7% across the three groups. Kidney function was preserved for those undergoing ESWL and renal function deteriorated in 1/15 studies with URS and 4/16 PCNL studies.

In an RCT of 68 patients with staghorn calculi, transperitoneal laparoscopic pyelolithotomy performed better than PCNL for stone-free rate (85.3% vs. 64.7%) but was associated with longer operative times (196.55 ± 26.58 minutes vs. 110.88 ± 34.82 minutes).

Mini-PCNL uses a smaller sheath size compared to standard PCNL (14-20 F vs. 24-30 F). Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 trials including 11 RCTs with 2567 patients treated with mini-PCNL and 2386 patients treated with standard-PCNL found no difference in stone-free rates and postoperative pain between the two procedures. Patients in the mini-PCNL group had significantly shorter hospital stays, less hemoglobin drop, less blood transfusion, higher postoperative tubeless, and fewer complications. Stone sizes in the respective trials varied from 16.38 to 42.8 mm. These findings were confirmed in a more recent meta-analysis of 16 RCTs in which mini-PNL had similar efficacy to PCNL in terms of stone-free rates, but had a superior safety profile with fewer overall complications and a reduced need for blood transfusion.

Minimally-invasive PCNL was superior to RIRS in another meta-analysis of 8 RCTs involving 725 patients with upper urinary stones for stone-free rate (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.05-1.17) but with a higher incidence of hematoma and longer hospital stay.

In a more recent meta-analysis including 21 RCTs comparing RIRS, SWL and mini-PCNL for patients with lower pole stone with a maximal diameter ≤20 mm, mini-PCNL had the highest stone-free rate and lowest retreatment rate but also the highest complication rate. For stones <10 mm, stone-free rates were similar for RIRS and SWL but retreatment was higher with SWL. Similar results were reported in a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs including 1674 patients with lower calyceal stones of 20 mm or less. In this study, ESWL was inferior to PCNL, mini- PCNL, ultramini-PCNL, and RIRS for efficacy, but superior to all but ultramini-PCNL for safety.

In an RCT of 220 patients with 1 to 2 cm lower-pole renal calculi randomly assigned to flexible ureteroscopy lithotripsy (FURL) or miniaturized PCNL, complications and stone-free rates were comparable between groups but blood loss, post-operative pain, and hospital stay were significantly lower in the FURL group. In another RCT including 101 patients with 1-2-cm intrarenal stones, mini-PCNL was more likely to render patients stone-free than FURL (76% vs. 46%, respectively).

For patients with larger stones (>=20 mm), authors of a network meta-analysis of 10 RCTs with 2917 patients concluded that mini-PCNL and standard PCNL were more effective treatment options than RIRS (86%, 86% and 79% stone-free rates, respectively), but were associated with higher complication rates compared to RIRS (16%, 32% and 11%, respectively); patients undergoing RIRS also had the shortest length of hospital stay.

In a prospective, first-in-human clinical trial, preliminary investigations revealed that the combined robotic-assisted mini-PCNL and flexible ureteroscopy procedure was successful in 12 of 13 procedure in terms of safety, efficacy and feasibility.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and 4 non-randomized studies of micropercutaneous surgery (smallest sheath size) found Microperc associated with fewer double-J stent insertions and higher stone-free rates compared to RIRS, but a greater drop in hemoglobin and longer hospital stay.

In an RCT of 175 patients with 1 to 2 cm lower calyceal stones randomized to five different procedures, stone-free rates were lowest in the RIRS and micro PCNL groups at 76% and 77% respectively, and comparable in the ultra-mini PNL, mini PNL, and standard PCNL groups at 90.1%, 94.1% and 94%, respectively. Length of hospital stay of 1 day and time to work return of 3.9 days, however, were shorter in the RIRS group; standard PCNL had the longest length of hospital stay of 3 days and time to return to work of 13.5 days.
In a prospective, multicenter-based RCT of 140 patients, radiation free RIRS was found to be noninferior to radiation usage RIRS for stones that were 20mm or smaller.

Single dose perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis is often given for PCNL; in one RCT of 191 subjects, sulbactam-ampicillin and cefuroxime were equally effective in preventing infection with similar positive culture rates and two cases of urosepsis. Single dose administration was sufficient.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies found that single dose antibiotic prophylaxis for PCNL was as effective as extended-dose antibiotic therapies for fever but extended-dose regimens were more effective for preventing systemic inflammatory response syndrome (OR = 1.81, 95% CI 1.30-2.53, I2 = 53%), especially in high-risk patients.

Administration of tranexamic acid in patients undergoing PCNL reduces both drop in hemoglobin, bleeding complications and transfusion rate (ORs 0.65, 0.32, and 0.34, respectively) based on a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs including 1262 patients.
Warm (37°) vs. cold or room temperature irrigation fluid during PCNL significantly reduces shivering and post-operative pain.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs including 831 patients found no evidence that ureteral stents reduced recurrent renal colic or stricture. There was a greater risk of lower urinary symptoms such as dysuria or urgency in patients who had a stent in place. AUA recommends against routine placement of stents prior to ureteroscopy.

The European Association of Urology 2021 guideline recommends against placement of postoperative stents following ureteroscopy or nephrostomy tubes after uncomplicated PCNL. In an RCT including 72 patients with proximal ureteral or renal stones undergoing uncomplicated ureteroscopy, those in the stented group had more irritative urinary symptoms and pain and missed more days of work (p < 0.01) that those who were not stented. Emergency room visits and overall complication rates were similar between groups. Three unstented patients required stent placement and two stented patients required early stent removal. Urinary tract infections developed in three stented patients, but not in unstented patients
Nephrectomy can be performed in patients with a negligible-functioning kidney requiring stone treatment.
Cranberry juice decreases oxalate and phosphate excretion and increases citrate excretion.
Limited evidence from two studies supports use of herbal therapy with Phyllanthus niruri to reduce kidney stone size and number.
In a RCT of 115 ED patients with renal colic, acupuncture was associated with a much faster and deeper analgesic effect and a better tolerance profile in comparison to titrated IV morphine.
Clinicians may offer continued surveillance to patients with asymptomatic, non-obstructing kidney stones.
Local warming to the back and abdomen with a heating pad reduces renal colic pain.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 304 patients with staghorn stones managed conservatively reported that disease-specific mortality ranged from 0% to 67% (mean 20.5%); progressive renal deterioration occurred in 0 to 100% (mean 27.5%), especially among patients with bilateral disease (44% vs. 9%); dialysis was required in 9% (20% bilateral, 6% unilateral); mean rate of severe infection was 8.7%; and recurrent urinary tract infections occurred in up to half of cases.
The medical management of urinary calculi is summarized in .

Increased fluid intake is usually recommended to facilitate stone passage. Authors of a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis found that for each 500 mL increase in water intake there was a significantly reduced risk of kidney stone formation (RR 0.93; 95% CI, 0.87-0.98).

Despite the potential benefit on stone passage of high fluid volume therapy and diuretics, authors of a Cochrane review of two studies found no reliable evidence to support this practice on improved pain or rate of surgical stone removal.

In an RCT of 100 patients presenting to the emergency department with renal colic, TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) resulted in greater degrees of clinically meaningful pain reduction than sham TENS. Pain ratings from a baseline of 70 and 72/100 at 15 and 30 minutes were 40/100 and 10/100 compared with 60/100 and 60/100 for those receiving sham therapy.
Hospitalization may be necessary for patients unable to tolerate or unresponsive to oral pain medications.

Surgical intervention is recommended with an obstructed urinary tract manifested by reduced urine output, fever, pyuria, and bacteria. Also consider intervention when patients have unrelenting pain not controlled by oral or IV pain medications.

Overall complication rates for ureteroscopy range from 9% to 25%, although most are listed as minor. Infectious complications, including urinary tract infections and urosepsis, account for about half of the complications and can be reduced by antibiotic prophylaxis, treatment of pre-operative UTI, and low procedural time.
Approximately 90% of ureteric stones less than 5 mm pass spontaneously, compared with 50% between 5 and 10 mm.
Fifty percent of patients have a second stone within 10 years, and 80% have at least one additional stone within 20 to 30 years.
Approximately 90% of ureteric stones less than 5 mm pass spontaneously, compared with 50% between 5 and 10 mm. Eighty percent of stones less than 4 mm pass in 1 to 2 weeks.

Authors of a secondary analysis of a multi-center prospective RCT with 382 evaluable patients diagnosed by CT scan with a symptomatic ureteral stone <9 mm found patient-report of stone passage to be highly accurate at 93.8% among the 97 patients (62%) reporting stone passage who returned for follow-up CT. Of patients who did not report stone passage, 72.1% (101/140) demonstrated passage of their stone on follow-up CT.
An observation period of 3 to 4 weeks is reasonable unless signs of obstruction or infection (fever, dysuria) occur.

In a retrospective study of 347 patients with asymptomatic renal stones, over one quarter passed the stones and about half had a symptom related to the stone 19 months following diagnosis. Although about one quarter of the patients required intervention, only 4.6% needed surgery.

Fewer difficulties were reported in a case series of 110 patients with 160 asymptomatic non-obstructing renal calculi followed for 41 ± 19 months. In this study, 28% of the stones became symptomatic, 3 stones caused silent obstruction necessitating intervention, and 17.4% passed spontaneously. Upper pole/mid renal stones were more likely than lower pole stones to become symptomatic and to pass spontaneously.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies of patients with asymptomatic renal stones found a risk of symptomatic episodes ranging from 0% to 59.4%, risk of admission from 14% to 19% and risk of intervention from 12% to 35% over a mean follow-up of at least 24 months. There were no significant differences in the likelihood of developing symptoms when comparing smaller and larger stones.
Stones recur in 50% of patients within 10 years and 80% in 20 to 30 years.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 40 retrospective studies and 13 prospective studies, including 488,130 patients, identified 12 risk factors associated with stone recurrence - younger age (n = 18 studies), higher BMI (n = 16), family history of kidney stones (n = 12), personal history of kidney stones (n = 11), hypertension (n = 5), uric acid stone (n = 4), race of Caucasian (n = 3), suspected kidney stone episode before the first confirmed stone episode (n = 3), surgery (n = 3), any concurrent asymptomatic (non-obstructing) stone (n = 2), pelvic or lower pole kidney stone (n = 2), and 24 h urine test completion.

In a study of endoscopic removal of ureteral or contralateral kidney stones in which 38 patients were randomized to removal of remaining small, asymptomatic stones and 35 to observation of similar-size, asymptomatic stones (control group), risk of relapse was lower in the treatment group (16% vs. 63%) over a mean follow-up of 4.2 years. Treatment added a median of 25.6 minutes to the surgery.

In patients undergoing PCNL the stone-free rate can be predicted using a nomogram based on stone burden, case volume, prior stone treatment, staghorn stone, stone location and stone count (area under the curve 0.76). In a comparison study of three prediction scoring systems—Guy score, S.T.O.N.E. score and CROES nomogram—authors found that all predicted stone-free status and the Guy and S.T.O.N.E. scores also predicted blood loss and length of stay.
Order radiographs every 1 to 2 weeks to follow retained stones.
Instruct patients to strain the urine to obtain a stone for analysis.

The AUA (2014/2019), based on expert opinion, recommends a single 24-hour urine specimen for stone risk factors within 6 months of initial treatment to assess response to therapy and again annually or with greater frequency, depending on stone activity, to assess patient adherence and metabolic response.
Periodic blood testing should be performed to assess for adverse effects in patients on pharmacological therapy.
For patients not responding to initial treatment, a repeat stone analysis, when available, should be obtained.
Monitor patients with struvite stones for reinfection with urease-producing organisms and utilize strategies to prevent such occurrences.
Periodic follow-up imaging is recommended by the AUA to assess for stone growth or new stone formation based on stone activity (plain abdominal imaging, renal ultrasonography or low-dose CT).
The clinical course and manifestation are similar in geriatric patients to that of younger patients.
There is an increased risk of stones formed from uric acid and due to hyperparathyroidism.

The pooled incidence of kidney stones is 0.49% or one case for every 204 pregnancies based on a meta-analysis of 9 studies including approximately 4.7 million pregnancies. In this analysis, kidney stones during pregnancy were significantly associated with development of preeclampsia, UTI, low birth weight, preterm labor, and C-section deliveries.
The clinical course and manifestation of kidney stones are similar in both pregnant and nonpregnant women.
Nearly all (99%) cases occur during the second or third trimester.
To avoid radiation exposure, renal US is recommended as the initial test.
When US is negative (sensitivity of 60%) and clinical suspicion is high, consider IVP or ureteroscopy.
In pregnant women, 75% to 80% of stones pass spontaneously.

AUA recommends observation in pregnant patients with ureteral stones and well-controlled symptoms. Ureteroscopy is offered to patients who fail observation, with a ureteral stent and nephrostomy tube available as alternative options; frequent stent or tube changes are usually necessary.

The classic presentation of flank pain is less common in children; 50% of children experience some form of abdominal or pelvic pain. Infants may present with colic. Between 33% and 90% of children have gross or microscopic hematuria.
Hypercalciuria is the most common metabolic cause in children.

Other metabolic causes include: (1) familial idiopathic hypercalciuria; (2) hyperuricosuria caused by cyanotic congenital heart disease, myeloproliferative disorders, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and type I glycogen storage disorders; (3) hyperoxaluria caused by primary hyperoxaluria types I and II; and (4) cystinuria caused by a disorder of renal tubular transport resulting in excessive excretion of the dibasic amino acids cystine, arginine, lysine, and ornithine.
In a large inpatient database study, hypertension and diabetes were associated with pediatric kidney stone disease among children younger than 6 years.

Initial imaging in cases of pediatric urolithiasis is US; non-contrast CT is the second option based on a systematic review and update on behalf of the European Association of Urologists by the urolithiasis guidelines panel.

Based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies, sensitivity of US for pediatric renal stones is 0.80 (95% CI, 0.70-0.87), specificity 1.00 (95% CI, 0.84-1.00), with an area under the curve of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.92-0.96).

AUA recommends offering observation, with or without α-blockers, for children with uncomplicated ureteral stones ≤10 mm. Ureteroscopy or ESWL can be offered to children with ureteral stones unlikely to pass or in whom observation has failed. As with adults, children with a total renal stone burden >20 mm can be offered either percutaneous nephrolithotomy or ESWL. Continued surveillance can be offered for those with asymptomatic and non-obstructing renal stones.

The European urolithiasis guidelines panel recommends consideration of expectant management for single, asymptomatic lower pole renal stone, especially in patients with non-struvite, non-cystine stones <7 mm. Recommended first line treatment is ESWL for renal stones <20 mm and for ureteral stones <10 mm followed by semi-rigid ureteroscopy, flexible ureteroscopy (for stones <20 mm), and PCNL for stones >20 mm.

In a RCT of 87 children with radiolucent renal calculi of 7 to 24 mm, similar stone-free rates were seen for dissolution therapy (potassium sodium hydrogen citrate at 1 mEq/kg per day for 1-3 months) vs. single session shock wave lithotripsy (72.9% vs. 82.1%, respectively).
In an RCT of 120 children with renal pelvic stone undergoing ESWL, there was no difference in stone clearance with the addition of tamsulosin. All children were cleared of stones after two sessions.
Authors of the systematic review noted above reported stone-free rates with ESWL of 70% to 90%, retreatment rates 4% to 50% and complication rates up to 15%.
In a retrospective study of 70 children treated with ESWL, after a mean of 11 years follow-up, there was no effect on growth and no child had developed hypertension or diabetes.
Slow delivery rates of shock wave lithotripsy vs. fast delivery rates provided better stone clearance in children with renal stones (90% vs. 73.3%, respectively) in one RCT.

In an RCT including 100 children aged 2-16 years with radio-opaque renal pelvic stones <20 mm, there was no significant difference in success rates and stone-free rates after one month between US-guided and fluoroscopic-guided ESWL.

Based on the systematic review by the European urolithiasis guidelines panel, semi-rigid ureteroscopy has stone-free rates of 81% to 98%, re-treatment rates of 6.3% to 10% and complication rates of 1.9% to 23%. Figures for flexible ureteroscopy are similar with stone-free rates of 76% to 100%, retreatment rates of 0% to 19% and complication rates of 0% to 28%.

Retrograde intrarenal surgery via semi-rigid ureteroscope compared to ESWL had similar outcomes with respect to safety and stone-free rate after a single session and at 3 months for treating medium sized renal stones in an RCT of 60 preschool children. Mean operative time was longer (40 ± 7.8 vs. 27.9 ± 3.5 minutes) as was mean hospital stay (12 ± 8 vs. 6 ± 2 hours) for intrarenal surgery while mean fluoroscopy exposure time was longer for ESWL (60 ± 42 and 50 ± 35 seconds).

Flexible ureteroscopy has a significantly higher stone-free rate than shock wave lithotripsy, with no difference in complication rate or fluoroscopy exposure time, and significantly higher operative times and hospital stay. However, the current evidence base for this is weak and further randomized trials are needed.
Stone-free rates with this procedure are 70.1% to 97.3% with an overall complication rate of 20% based on the systematic review by the European urolithiasis guidelines panel.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 studies suggest that percutaneous nephrolithotomy is more effective than retrograde intrarenal surgery for treatment of larger kidney stones (>20 mm) in children due to its higher stone-free rate. Retrograde intrarenal surgery, however, may result in shorter hospital stays.

For treatment of large or complex renal stones in children, percutaneous nephrolithotomy monotherapy had better stone-free rates (95.5% vs. 71% for intrarenal surgery), while retrograde intrarenal surgery had less radiation exposure and was associated with fewer complications and shorter hospital stay in one RCT.
